The phoenix soars from the celestial cliffs; the five-colored qilin gallops forth. Since it has attained its place, there can be no partiality; when it is employed, there shall be no distinction between the distant and the near.
Returning to my old garden, the autumn light is beautiful; cassia seeds scatter their fragrance, and chrysanthemum buds are fresh.

He transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in blood; for the Elder Shouning’an, he inscribed the title of the Great Canon of the *Avataṃsaka*, placing it above all other expositions. To complete this transcription by shedding his own blood was no small karmic affinity.

In a mere instant, it pervaded over a hundred cities; the practices of three asaṃkhyeya kalpas were perfected in a single lifetime. The myriad peaks suddenly fell away as Mount Sumeru rose high; the multitude of luminaries withdrew their brilliance as the sun blazed forth.
The sun hangs suspended; I laugh at how Sudhana spent his efforts in vain. He traveled south until his soles were worn through.

Sent to Brother Monk Fanhuan, I am filled with shame that I have inherited the mantle of Mount Jing. I envy your lofty character, which I cannot match; the pure breeze flows vast and wide from the Southern Hall.

Far away, the ancient road stretches on as the accumulated greens return. He does not speak of the "illnesses of Chan," yet his spiritual capacity is naturally lofty; his compassionate countenance remains unchanged, though his hair has turned white.
Even the Buddha-flower tree has recently returned to the Eastern Monastery; heaven and earth can accommodate the leisure of these two elders.
In the same rhyme, I respond to the previous occasion:
Master Chengyupuo sweeps the quiet gate at the depths of Lake Xi. The Patriarchs and Buddhas have no mind with which to act further. Detached from marks, one is originally detached from nature;
Ultimately, there is neither Chan nor teacher. Where the wind arises and shakes the bamboo on the empty eaves, The moon emerges as the clouds part over the distant ridges.
At this supreme time, the myriad phenomena blaze forth, constantly expounding the Dharma. Why does the mountain elder need to break off pine branches?
To the Abbot Xizang of Tianjie:
where the golden cock crows, one penetrates the profound mechanism; shifting keys and modulations, let them be applied as you please. How could learning not be something extraordinary?

In study, the conditioned is ultimately no different from the unconditioned. The manifestation of lands upon the tip of a hair is not originally marvelous; writing scriptures in empty space is not yet extraordinary.
Raise up the dialogue beyond the Night-Bright Curtain: the *udumbara* flower blooms upon a branch that has never sprouted.
Venerable Chang, you are fundamentally free from duality; why use further deliberation? You have cut off the path of sound and words, and the light behind your head blazes forth.
How bitter is the heart of Zhuan-an! How long is the tongue of Fo-yen! I, this old man, am exceedingly indolent; who can shake out my bowels of dung?
When the first attendant held up a tuft of cloth, who could follow its flash? To hesitate is to create an obstacle; to deliberate further involves doubt.
At Longtan’s place where the candle was extinguished, and when Deshao lifted the curtain—thrown once beyond the other world, the lanterns spread their smiling brows.
Showing his brilliance, Attendant Jun broke the fan and sought the rhinoceros. Yan Guan was not skilled at planning; he could only act with spontaneous disregard for convention.

Finding elegance wherever he went, he sought fire from the bottom of clear waves and struck the whale at the top of the green trees. Though the Northern Mountain is stubborn, it too will roll its eyes for you.
In the same rhyme, I answer my elder brother Dharma-master Zhao’an of former Beichan:
A true scion of the Xi clan, wherever he touches, he displays the soaring hawk; he holds aloft the mirror within his breast, casting a slanting radiance from behind his crown.

Wind and clouds conceal his staff and sandals; rivers and seas have satiated him through many autumns and winters. When he ascends the high seat, his methods of practice are uniquely skillful. To Xie Guan:
Regarding the ritual for the precepts at Mount Nanyue, the hair-pen has not yet been raised;
once the text of the precepts is finished, how could it tolerate the assembly of Tan Di? Daoxuan is not permitted to pass through.
Grasping at signs results in further obstruction; even a mindless state still leaves traces behind. Where the incense first spreads from the burner, Mount Nanyue towers in the clear sky.
To cultivate the Way, one should diminish daily. Next, Puming [Monastery] revives the melodic lineage of this school:
eating when hungry and wearing clothes when cold, responding to circumstances as they arise. When in meditation, sit without a deliberate mind; when reciting sutras, do so without intentional focus.

The springtime light departs of its own accord; the flowing waters follow their course to the east. Who would say that the teachings of a thousand years are as precarious as a single thread supporting the Nine Cauldrons?

This was given to the Abbot Yuanzang as a silent response to the question of a monk regarding characters: "The Great Canon is truly difficult to expound. How can one who is dull-witted receive it? How can one who is clever receive its transmission?"
Do not add specks of dust to the eyes; sow the field within the ears well. Transcending far beyond the time of Wei-yin, the autumn sky and the night moon are full.
To show this marvel, O Attendant:
the extraordinary matters of our school are ultimately beyond words and thought. Even this "is" is still not "is"; even the one who knows does not truly know.
Do not pass on the meditation board; cease waiting for the whisk of fur to blow. Seeing it atop the Black Stone Ridge, why was your response so late?
To Master Zhen, I show: Smash the pearl within the treasury; its radiance dazzles the great void. Open the true eye at the crown of the head; cast off the numinous talisman from behind the elbow.

When delusion is obliterated, truth is also obliterated; the mind is as such, and the objects of the mind are likewise. At the critical ford, one lightly cuts it off; the old shaggy beard is knocked over.
*The Recorded Sayings of National Teacher Nan-shih*, Volume Three;
*The Recorded Sayings of National Teacher Nan-shih*, Volume Four.
Compiled by the Disciples, including Ryōteki and others.
Verses on the Buddha’s Birth, Part Two.
As soon as he emerged from the womb, he was already full of self-importance; he strode about, needlessly flaunting his vital spirit. This fellow is originally but a traveler of the wind and dust;
take care not to call out for a washbasin in broad daylight.
A stone cliff stands upright in mid-air, ten thousand fathoms high. How many people have rubbed their foreheads in vain toil?
To know that the perilous place is as level as a whetstone, one must cast off all attachments and arrive there in person.
I visited Master Zhongxing at Luyin Spring, an old master of the Way. Why would he not ascend to Longhua? When I came to meet him, there was no speech;
he merely inquired after my well-being, burned incense, and then we drank tea.
Presented to Chan Master Xizang of Fusang for Beating the Heishan Drum at Huqiu: The Haoyong Peak studies the Linji Chan; He splits asunder the Three Mysteries and Two Essentials.
The wind shakes the river willows, green as mist.
The Ghost-Seer’s Verse Beneath the Vairocana Pavilion: All you Chan practitioners of the four seas should know this well: Having examined it thoroughly, it turns out to be but a single phrase;
Yet if one speaks of that single phrase, doubt is already formed.
Sent from Former Ever-Remembrance Hall, Contemplating Non-Self (at that time residing at Jinghui Hermitage):
These windows and these walls all record the mind. Deceiving ordinary people with deep stratagems. The pillar before the hall opens its living eye;
On the high mountains and flowing waters, there is one who understands.
Within the shout there is both guest and host; within the breast there is neither self nor other.
These seventeen hundred years of ancient talk—directly uprooted, it is the springtime of the path of speech.
Sent from Illness to Huantianzhang and Other Illustrious Friends:

The body is originally empty; who is it that suffers illness? Illness has no body to receive it; the suffering itself is empty. At this moment, there is nowhere for cognition or understanding to abide.
Beyond the shore, the slanting sun reflects red upon the water.
Smoke curls from the stone bench; incense wafts from the tile stove. Among the thousand sages, they measure one another's length and breadth.
Two mouths indeed possess not a single tongue; do not let this news reach all quarters.
A grand descendant of Linji, pressing heavy and lifting light to open the crown of the head;
with these flavorless words, pierced through in every way, what prevents one from chewing them to pieces and swallowing the whole lump?
Presented to Chan Master Wanshou Da:
Restraining the monastic community, its atmosphere is renewed; the golden-maned lion knows how to turn its body.
Casually drawing forth the sword between his brows, he startles the earth-spirits of Jambudvīpa.
Presented to Abbot Yan:
The ancient teachings illuminate the mind; the mind itself is luminous. Do not mistake the handle of a grain for the stalk of rice.
Deshan saw only the Old Man of Longtan; poison and nectar are practiced as one path.

As the South Venerable departs, before the Buddha was born, he struck once with his mallet. To "carve the boat to seek the sword" is nothing short of tardy. Fortunately, at the head of his feet, he possesses the eye that knows the way;
would he ever deign to learn like an ordinary child groping for a path?
The ocean of mind is formless, signless, and nameless; the myriad phenomena are all clearly sealed by a single mark. The Buddhas find it difficult to fathom its depth or shallowness;
from ancient times to the present, people have mistakenly called it the vast blue sea.

The portrait of Master Ying’an, whom Mei Yang especially cherished as he returned to the ancient source. He was able to ensure that the true lineage of Yangqi remained unbroken. Those of later generations do not understand the intention of the former masters;
they merely establish their own sectarian styles beneath the *buddhagarbha*.

He Chèn says: Whether dwelling in a mountain retreat or staying in a monastery, it matters not whether the hermitage is large or small; in all cases, one simply requires that the "medicine" be efficacious.
If Master Xiang does not descend from the peak of Lotus Mountain, his cool words and idle talk are naturally worth listening to.

Without hesitation, he personally grasps the handle of the ladle; entering the water, what prevents him from further entering the mud? The conditions for the people and officials of the coastal lands have already ripened;
let it be well that each and every one shall reach Caoqi.
Sending Jian to reside at the Dabaocaowu Hermitage in Xuancheng:
A solitary life in a thatched hut is no cause for shame; ten thousand granaries and myriad foundations are not true glory.
With the Vajra-eye protruding from the tip of his staff, he proclaims the practice of self-cultivation throughout Jambudvīpa.

While traveling on my mission of transformation, I spontaneously composed this verse on the first principle of the gateway of the six perfections: It is as bright as a thousand suns radiating its brilliance by day;
When meeting others, I do not hesitate to raise it again and again, Yet those among the people of this age who can truly comprehend it are rare.
Exhortation to Practice the Three Scriptures (with Preface).
In the eleventh year of the Hongwu era, His Majesty, amidst the leisure between the myriad affairs of state, took pity on us, his disciples who are followers of the Buddha.
Observing that few among us were able to master the scriptural teachings or deeply investigate the study of Chan, he specially issued an imperial decree to have us practice them.
Day and night, he lectured on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya*, the *Vajracchedikā*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, and practiced seated meditation, striving to achieve profound understanding.
Is he not indeed an emanation of an ancient Buddha who has come to propagate the teachings?

I, the monk Wenxiu, sincerely fear that my fellow practitioners may be unable to look up to and uphold the Imperial intent through diligent study; therefore, I have composed these seven verses to encourage them.

Thus it was that the Sage Emperor personally received the sacred inscription from the Spirit Mountain; grasping the Golden Wheel, he governed the myriad regions and issued an edict to the monastic community to engage in study and practice,
whereby the monasteries suddenly became radiant with splendor.
In sealing the mind, let not the *Laṅkāvatāra* be surpassed for its subtlety; in washing away appearances, none is as intimate as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Once one realizes the true purport of these three sutras, the thousand reds and ten thousand purples are all but a single spring.
To fully comprehend the phrase of conditions and the phrase of non-conditions, one must recognize that true emptiness is fundamentally not empty.
Only when you have attained a transformed body capable of receiving the staff can I transmit this news to you.
The source of the Buddha-dharma is not easily fathomed; one must simply apply oneself with diligent effort day and night.
Once the meaning at the head of the sutra is seen through, a path opens even through iron walls and silver mountains.
Once you have attained the essential meaning, you must ensure that your vision is not biased. Chan is not a different teaching from the scriptures, and the scriptures are no different from Chan.
Like a group of blind men feeling an elephant and describing its various features, how could they ever grasp the elephant in its entirety?
The commentators each uphold their own school; there is difference within sameness and sameness within difference.
One should simply grasp the intent of the Tathāgata himself, rather than falling into the trap of ordinary, dead words.

The thorough study of the scriptural teachings and the practice of Zen meditation are matters of great significance, not minor ones. Fortunately, we have encountered a sagacious sovereign who can pay close attention;
why, then, should we, his followers, fail to apply ourselves with greater diligence?
Viewing Flowers, Shown to Yang Yuxuan:
I have come unexpectedly to the eastern courtyard and lean against the balustrade. Red and white flowers bloom in a tapestry of brocade. I cherish most the fine words of Nanquan;
People of this age view them only as a dream.

I sent the repository keeper Ying, the practitioner Haiyun, to the riverbank. During our night conversation, I learned that my elder brother was at Haiyun; it was indeed the very place where we had met eight years ago.
Beneath the true pine trees, the first glow of twilight fell.
To Master Jingyuan:

In old age, he has forgotten all worldly affairs; let the rising and setting of the sun and moon be as they may in their bustle. Eating his meals and wearing his robes as circumstances require, he passes his days without a single thought of the Western Paradise.
The seven-axle numinous text, a single curl of incense smoke; in this quiet chamber, all worldly ties are exhausted.
At nightfall, as the lamp dims and mice and insects emerge, the tea scoop falls over onto the edge of the bed.
A Self-Description by One Dwelling on the River, Sent to Yuan-yi Zong-ping:
I am dull-witted and incompetent in a hundred ways; I have built a thatched hut upon the fishing banks.
With a rustic wooden bed and a yew-wood pillow, I often sleep through the night until the break of dawn.

The Sage Emperor did not forget the records of the Spirit Mountain; by imperial decree, he raised up forest monasteries and monks of the Way. Seated high upon the great dais, they expounded the Great Dharma;
indeed, they have succeeded in continuing the lamp of Shaolin.
In my secluded study, the door is closed alone as the day deepens into dusk. Emerald hues float upon the steps, where mossy patterns encroach.
Having dwelt by the riverbank for ten years now, who in this world understands the heart of one on the Way?
The patriarch’s verse stuck to the wall has been blown down by the wind; spiderwebs caught on the eaves are opened by the rain. Green shadows fill the paths as the flowers have all fallen away;
not a single bird has ever come before the gate.
The single room is vast and silent, the autumn night long; I sit at ease alone upon my worn wooden bench. Clearly there is a phrase that cannot be uttered;
The river moon and pine-wind raise it up of their own accord.
To urge others to build houses is the business of a layman; to pile three feet of mud upon level ground is to act like one who knows not that the Tathāgatas of the three periods have never been thus.
To raise chickens is with the intent that they crow at the fifth watch.
The tiger is tamed as it stands in the path; Third Uncle Zhai is present. Ghosts assist in founding the base; Master Xiang is there. A single expanse of river light is pure as a silken brocade.
Leaning on the railing, standing alone at the hour of the setting sun.
In the same rhyme, I answer Master Bó'ān:
Wherever he goes, fire burns through ice; how can he be contained within the seat of a master-monk? This is the true seedling of the papaya tree;
its radiance shines like a lamp before the kalpas.

The shadows of consciousness and its objects have long since dissolved; how could the turmoil of the myriad realms invade? Sitting and cutting off past and present, emptiness transcends Buddhas and patriarchs;
the ocean wind pushes the moon up to the heart of heaven.

Throughout the Patriarchal Hall, everywhere is shrouded in wind and dust; even an iron-stone heart is moved to sorrow. Only one who possesses the hand that can unfurl the great net and grasp the essential principles—know that such must be a person from south of the Dipper.

A small pavilion amidst dense bamboos by the great river’s edge; the rains have fallen and spring deepens, as the bamboo shoots and ferns grow plump. Five-colored clouds arrive from beyond the heavens;
a pair of cranes return toward the treetops.

In the same rhyme, sent to Hui Xingquan on practicing the Way and guiding disciples—Part Two: Thatched roof and bamboo couch, all worldly ties stilled; The devas and Brahmās come with no path to offer flowers;
Vastly distant white clouds, a thousand acres of autumn.
In the same rhyme, a reply to Faxinghai upon his departure:
Sitting opposite him by the hearth, I stir the cold ashes; A single cry of wild geese comes from across the sea.
Since I have not encountered anyone here like you, I have opened my thatched gate wide throughout the night.
Sent to my Dharma brother Duke Shou from Du’an at Dingjiasi Temple, recounting our parting: Just as the yellow oriole cries out beyond the willows, I count the years that have passed—now ten.
The frost upon my temples must surely be heavier than it was then.
A sudden turn upon that very pivot—when meeting anyone, I urge them exclusively to recite the name of Amitābha.
In years past, when Bian Que went to Xianyang, he spoke only of his unique ability to treat infants.
The disciple has composed this poem on the Pure Land; from three thousand *li* away, it is sent to the riverbank. Strike the sounding block and invite all the monks to look:
a brilliant rainbow light pierces through my humble robes.
Autumn comes, and the waters of Wu are unsurpassed in their clarity; the clouds clear from Mount Yan, and the moon shines even brighter.
Even if one were to say that the hearts of brothers are beyond questioning, one would know they have not yet transcended ordinary sentiment.
Seeing off a Monk for Jingshan (The circumstances of this verse were that it was sent to Lü Jingfu; therefore, I have added commentary beneath each line).

Five-crested Peak towers high, piercing the azure heavens—(Even the thousand sages look up at it but cannot reach it. For many years not a single person has been seen to travel there—(One can see that such decorum is appropriate.

The Way-seeking traveler’s ambition and spirit swallow the rainbows and halos—(I only fear he may not be jade. With staff in hand, he pierces the clouds to reach the summit—(I do not yet dare grant him my full approval.)
A wild boat is moored at the head of a stony rapid (this is not yet the moment of arriving home). Mountain clouds are vast and the trees are dark green (what a fine message!).

Master Qin’s countenance is clearly present (take care not to mistake the donkey’s saddle-bridge for your father’s chin). Though you see it, it remains as it was—still not quite right (the mysterious barrier has yet another hundred thousand layers).
Inscribed on Blood:
The Eight Returns to Discern the Seeing and the Seven Investigations of the Mind. A needle is driven straight into the painful spot of weary life;
With a light stroke across the tip of a single hair, The morning frost covers the red leaves throughout Donglin.
Bestowing [this] upon Zhou Daocheng at Dao Shan:
It lies precisely within the ordinary activities of daily life; how could it abide in the north, south, east, or west?
Zhaozhou points out that which is beyond the wall—how much more so than a peak ten thousand fathoms high!
In the same rhyme, I send off Master Zang:
Shattering that final barrier of the profound mystery, the thousand streams and ten thousand coves all flow toward the source. Deshan burned the Dragon River Memorial;
like mosquitoes in the void, they stir against a fierce wind.

Without a mirror, how could a single dharma have ever been established from the outset? This very vessel of manifestation leaves nothing behind. Yet one laughs at the Twin Trees still having a reflection;
they still come to the water to observe their own heads.
Entrusted with the profound Dharma-treasury, Daowei propagates the Way in Eastern Wu; the Chan teachings are indeed desolate. It is a joy to see the dais opened within this ancient Buddha-field.
Boundless bhikṣus gather in competition, their left shoulders bared as they listen to the exposition.

The Abbot sends this to the Venerable Vinaya Master, a master from all quarters who has offered gifts to the Vinaya Master: The steamed rice and peach blossoms are served in abundance; I, Wanshou, cannot follow the common custom.
Let us serve tea together as we descend the front slope.
When Master Mowei heard the sound of a wooden hoop being struck on a cloud peak, he mistakenly took it for the kitchen fire-board ringing. He laughed at how even Cuoyan remained so clumsy;
this morning, he came forth specifically to greet him with a smile.

The sculpted figures of the Buddhas of the Three Ages and the tableau of people practicing mindfulness of the Buddha present a majestic array of marks and signs, like a mountain of purple gold. Yet it resides within the ordinary moment of a single thought.
To cause every person to personally pay them reverence, I have again troubled myself to fashion these forms for all to behold.
Xia’an presents this to Luo Juewu:
The moment he sees a flowering branch, his face breaks into a smile; Dharmatrāta was truly like one peering through a tube at a speck. How can he compare to sitting upright beneath a thatched eave?
Not a single bird comes; the spring day is leisurely and still.

This Mirror of Mind is bestowed upon Cai Miaojing, personally cast from within the furnace of the Dharma-nature. One knows with certainty that it is fundamentally not made of bronze. Vast and brilliantly clear, it pervades the entire realm of sand;
the myriad phenomena of the universe are reflected within its single illumination.
I conjure a long-lasting bright lamp;
one bowl of light illuminates the ancient Buddha hall. For years it has been radiant and magnificent.
Although it is inherently free from darkness, it must be further brought forth by people together.
Zongyuan presents this to Venerable Hai:
The vast expanse of the blue sea is profoundly deep and wide. Who says that the blue sea returns to this very place? Even Mañjuśrī would find it difficult to fathom its depths;
How could a child playing in a shallow stream ever know it?
Sending off the Abbot Meng of Shushan:
A wooden snake’s head lets loose the uncaused. Iron walls and silver mountains, ten thousand fathoms cold. With a single silence, he has already lightly brushed them aside;
let him wander at will through the three Wu regions and the hundred Yue lands.

As I see off the two Chan practitioners Jiao and Xi on their pilgrimage to Mount Emei to pay homage to Samantabhadra, they have accompanied me morning and night. What need is there for the labor of traveling so far to seek him? When one sees a milestone, one knows the road;
only then does one realize that he has never been away from Emei.
Emei’s peaks are like brocade-swept after the rains; the barefooted Persian has his nostrils pierced.
Waiting further for the Elephant King to appear from within the clouds, he still falls before the skull.
When Shifu the Venerable was granted a blow of the staff and fined, he was nonetheless expelled from the monastery. Yet, how profound was Xinghua’s stratagem!
Had he known it beforehand before I had even raised my hand, he would have already followed the warbling orioles past the willow shadows.
To the Attendant Gao:
To study the Way, one must first have lofty aspirations; then, carrying a rain-cane and wearing frost-worn sandals will not be in vain. Fortunately, the eye atop your head is as bright as the sun;
why wait for the wind from Mount Beishan to blow upon your hair?
In the same rhyme, I reply to Zhi-men Ze and Tian-lin:
The profound wind spreads far and wide across all quarters; When the Peerless Horse returns, the myriad steeds are empty.
Without raising the lotus flower or the lotus leaf, One naturally transcends the standard and surpasses the lineage.
Opening wide the gates to welcome the stream of Chan, what need is there to ask whether one comes from the South or the North? Directly and immediately, there is not the slightest concealment;
at White Rock, the clouds have cleared and the moon is like a hook.
Seeing off Attendant Nan of Huqiu for Linggu:
Within the voice of Little Jade, one finds the guiding direction. It was not in vain that you personally met Old Yunyan. Tomorrow morning, you will shake out your sleeves and depart for Zhongshan;
with a thousand li of east wind, you sail upon a single cloth sail.
An analysis of the verse by Venerable Xuguang (Hushan) for the lay practitioner Wu Jingwan:

"One's own mind is the Buddha"—few indeed take this up with resolve. "In every land and at every dust mote, precious light is emitted; at night one listens to the pines, in the morning one listens to the rain;
when cold comes, one turns toward the fire; when hot, one seeks the cool."
When mindfulness reaches the emptiness of mind, even the Buddha is forgotten; there remains nothing else to be pondered. Having awakened upon my wooden bed, the east is already bright;
the crimson sun shines radiantly upon the bamboo hermitage.
Seated, one cuts off one’s own true pure land; a nine-crested phoenix dances in the crimson heavens. The Yellow-Faced Gautama is not the Buddha;
the old bearded barbarian with missing teeth is surely not the Patriarch.
Where else could one seek the Western Land? The horse stable, the cow pen, and the site of perfect enlightenment—this decrepit old man, Quan’an, has stubbornly provided his commentary.
Clearly, he is merely gouging a sore upon healthy flesh.
The attendant Xian whom I have shown you as coming and going is the treasury. When cast forth at Dangyang, it is an iron Kunlun; with a casual blow, it shatters into a hundred fragments.
At midnight, the sun emerges from the sea gate.

When National Teacher Huizhong called his attendant Shiyi three times, and Shiyi responded to the National Teacher on three occasions, it was not a matter of Mount Sumeru being placed within a mustard seed;
it was clearly a matter of the mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru.
To the seamstress, he shows a single bolt of cloth sufficient for a great trichiliocosm; do you see it presented face-to-face?
Skillfully take the golden scissors and lightly cut it open, and fashion for me an *uttarāsaṅga*.
Shishi Weina said of Beishan, "He speaks words of truth. The Way lies within the ordinary activities of daily life; he transforms grain into charcoal as he returns.
This old fellow Cuiyan attained Yunfeng."
Sending off Venerable Jian as the *karmadāna* involved a fine and a beating; this was no ordinary matter. Only one with an iron-stone heart could have endured it.
Fortunately, Mount Beishan has had no such affairs, so there is no need for word to spread to all quarters.

Entrusting this to the joy of the Dharma and amidst mutual respect, I follow the precedent of eminent monks in the temple to discuss the profound mysteries. Counting on my fingers since then, another four years have passed. The autumn waters are as blue as indigo, and the mountains are like brushed eyebrows;
for this sealed letter, there is no need to rely on geese or fish to carry it.

A single peak of the quiet mountain stands solitary and towering; let the whirlwind blow from all eight directions as it may. Through kalpas and asaṃkhyeya aeons, through formation and destruction, it remains steadfastly unmoved by even a hair’s breadth.
To the attendant Wanshou Zong:
Chan-month precedes the mechanism; all mundane sentiments and sagely understandings are vast and empty. Nanyang called the attendant three times;
a damp paper was brought forth to wrap a tiger.
When the transformed tea enters my gate, one simply drinks it; its elegance transcends all standards and is truly worthy of praise.
Although there is not much to its application, to truly appreciate it, one must surely be a master.
To Attendant Xi: When hungry, eat;
when thirsty, drink; when weary, sleep. In daily life, everything is naturally manifest. To report to the assembly while wandering the corridors, you falsely fabricate strange tales.
At the gate of Shaolin, there has never been any Chan.
In the same rhyme, I respond to the farewell for Master Xiangjian’an;

the clergy and laity of the capital region all cry out in joy. Majestic and solitary like a spring-fed rock against the azure sky, he commands the full range of taking and giving, releasing and seizing, killing and enlivening;
his divine mechanism never yields to the strategies of Sun or Wu.
The Elder Brother’s wondrous understanding subdued the assembly of lords; he harmonized the myriad differences to reach Great Sameness.
North, south, east, and west—the heavens and earth are vast—and in every atom, the breeze of Shaolin is spread.
Sent to Venerable Xue of Chengtian:
At dawn on Mount Efu, the clouds hang thick; after the rain in Changzhou, the waters ripple across the marshes.
Where one smiles in welcome within the Hall of Green Rocks—how has it ever been different from this very moment?
Settling the mind reveals the center;
the rector is constantly present at the tip of a single hair. When both subject and object are forgotten, how can one observe?
It is laughable that Shen Guang was deluded regarding his own fundamental wondrousness, yet he followed the Patriarch to seek peace.
Seeing off Chan Master Xin at Wild Waters White Lotus: The vast ocean stretches afar; the lake and mountains rise in emerald peaks against the cold, azure sky.
This entire, undifferentiated Vairocana-realm—do not view it as a mere objective scene as you have done before.

An ancient stone beyond the limit of Vipaśyin, a single *paṭa* naturally perfected from the beginning, requiring no carving or polishing. Were one to further debate whether the mind is internal or external,
it would have already followed the Qin chariot past Silla.
The Head Seat Mingbai shaved his head and offered a donation to establish the karmic connection for ten thousand monks;

by establishing the connection for one monk, he established the connection for ten thousand. Before the Hall of Good Dharma, jeweled nets hang suspended. A single stroke of the "bitting the arrowhead" function can be employed in reverse;

Spontaneously Composed While Ill In sickness, meeting people makes me too weary to open the door. The wooden pillow at my bedside has never been shifted. I brew mountain tea in a small cauldron and burn cypress in the brazier;
My young attendant opens the gate for me and receives visitors.
Vimalakīrti lay ill in his chamber at Vaiśālī; the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī specifically to inquire after his health.
This became a famous anecdote throughout India and China, yet this old monk was ultimately not deceived by him.
Once feverish, once chills; head aches, waist pains, and bones ache. Seeking where the illness might have originated—wooden men clap their hands and dance upon the clouds.
I show that the Elder Guan Shuchun (Zhengyin) has already reached the mind of the original source; meeting circumstances and encountering conditions, he is able to shoulder his responsibility.
I laugh, however, at those who wander outside [the Way], all of whom end up carrying straw while discarding the golden treasure.
Bowing and rising, moving and turning, according to the moment—why falsely maintain a mind fixed on a single object? In leisure, I copy scriptures and still recite the Buddha’s name;
every single thing is entirely the Chan of Shaolin.
In the nine thoroughfares, men and horses rush about day after day; wealth, nobility, and fame fill the imperial capital. Having dwelt here for a long time, the mind becomes naturally steady;
Amitābha radiates light from every point of contact.
In years past we met by the banks of the Lianxi; today we meet again at the gates of Baixia.
Upon earthen mats and rush cushions, the pine fire grows cold; there is no Dharma whatsoever to discuss.
The Patriarch’s Stupa of the Eye of Dharma does not move the myriad phenomena;
yet it moves the myriad phenomena. A hawk flies ten thousand leagues to Silla; north of the lake, south of the Xiang, there is no place to find it.
Under the bright moon, the tide strikes the Stonehead Citadel.
Simply taking clarity as the Way is itself the achievement; seeing forms and hearing sounds, there is no need for deafness. Let all things proceed as they were before;
within words there is resonance, while the phrases conceal their sharp edges.
Dizang’s fingertip directly points it out; within a single speck of dust, the oceans of lands appear in full majesty.
Those seekers of the profound mystery south and north of the Yangtze River—listen as this is proclaimed before the Stūpa.
I bid farewell to Elder Wù as he departs to reside at Chóng'ēn;
the task of maintaining a mountain monastery is no easy matter. If you understand this, know that after many years, you will surely be able to achieve great things.
At Yàoqiǎo’s Ox-Stall, the fire from burning dung still shines with brilliance today, filling the entire realm.
The wild grasses flourish atop the mountain of the five aggregates; though passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, they have not yet been worn away.

Both eyes have grown dim and lost their clarity; my ears are blocked and my hair is matted and wild. Master Wu has long been skilled with the razor and scissors;
he recognizes this kind of dull-witted monk.
Before the hair has grown and the feet have even crossed the mountain gate, the sound of the golden tweezers reaches the very root of the ears. What a marvelous message for the benefit of others!
One does not know who among them can truly recognize this kindness.
Musing on Antiquity in the Mountains:
The carp atop the mountain, the dust at the bottom of the well—without cause, I have exhausted my aged spirit.
As one born late, I am entirely unable to trouble you; I am ashamed, yet I remain a fellow villager (Guoyi).
In our school, directness is prized above all verbal explanation. A hawk flies over the eighteen thousand li to Silla.
Who would say that within the vast and silent expanse of heaven and earth, after the Cloud-toothed One has passed, there are no sages (or: none are superior)?
Shining boots—let them shine as they will; when the mouth opens, how has a single tooth ever moved?
Even for a guest who possesses the discerning eye of the subtlest measure, the eggplant in the back garden has already blossomed. (Fajie)

He treats the Buddhas and Patriarchs with contempt and looks down upon all quarters. Grasping his bamboo staff upside down, who dares to face him? His calamities will plague his descendants until the end of time;
he deserves to be exiled to Mei Yang for the rest of his life. (Miaoxi)
The moon hovers over the mountain stream, its ripples a brilliant azure; The sun shines upon the solitary peak, its verdant hue ever fresh.
To call this the Patriarch’s profound and wondrous secret— One might wish to head for Eastern Lu, yet end up in Qin (Zhenxie).
The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is a broken sand pot; the Yellow River flows in nine bends from Kunlun. It is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor any thing;
it does not establish a family, but rather destroys it. (Miman)
Bestowing a sutra and building a pavilion are matters of utter indifference; that "the water reaches the ditch" is not yet the truth.
Only in the place where fists are raised in mutual exchange is there something clearly laughable and yet startling (Biefeng).
By special imperial decree, the banner was moved to Mount Jingshan. From time to time, he desired to behold the compassionate countenance.
Having once listened to the Dharma together on Vulture Peak, today he has returned once more to appear in this world (Fozhao).
A magnetic bowl from Qiongzhou and a begging bowl from Suizhou—its value is so great that nothing in the world can compare to it.
Do not say that people of the world do not recognize it; every time it is brought forth, it is ever new. (Wuzhun)
The eyes are triangular, resembling the eyebrows of a sorrowful barbarian; strange and wondrous, there is not a single thing understood.
He is accustomed to driving a three-legged donkey to turn the millstone—how could he ever appear on the patriarchal charts? (Zangyun)

The whale swallows the sea water, revealing the coral; having personally held the tally-stick, he ascended to the Imperial Capital. For a thousand ages, the Chan school remains as secure as its foundations;
who among the monastic groves recognizes the red-bearded one (Yunfeng)?
The Go-board Stone atop Mount Lingxiao—how many people’s foreheads has it split open?
If you seek it again from beneath words, you will merely end up marking the traces of a boat on the water after the sword has been lost. (Jizhao)
It is said that by investigating things, principle is attained, yet things are not constant; when things are investigated, who knows the path grows ever longer?
Had he not presented even half a verse before others, who would have known he could compose such grand literary works? (Zishao)
In Sanskrit it is called *ekapiṇḍa*; in the language of Tang, it means "to become a single mass. My family’s samādhi is known by the common people;
from now on, I shall no longer conceal my horns and tusks, but shall offer poems whenever I encounter a poet (Jichuan).

Sending off Secretary Ci:
Huanglong’s wrathful pillow was hurled at Yunfeng; it struck Ciming’s great "empty deception. Jingwu did not apply the three blows of the staff;
I vow to exert my strength and continue this lofty tradition.
Entrusting myself to Lu Juehai, our long-term retreat has reached its full term. Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—all have become Chan.
On the second month of spring by the Lou River, every strand of willow is laden with mist.
A Gift for Shen Boxiang (Upon Reading the Avataṃsaka Sūtra):
One can hear with the eyes and see with the ears; The myriad layers of the Flower Treasury World reside upon a single hair-tip.
That Sudhana traveled specifically to the south Was merely to be deceived by Mañjuśrī’s bitter heat.

Gathering clouds fly atop the Five Peaks; How could the jade of Bian or the pearls of Sui compare? Dragon-elephants fill the hall to gaze in competition;
The mountains of Yue and the waters of Wu are but empty excursions.
In the same rhyme, I reply to the former recommendation for Yan Zongzhuyuan:
A single mat in a quiet room beneath the ancient city wall; On a curved bench and round rush mat, one recognizes this mind. Your name shall be honored throughout heaven and earth across all time;
Zhaozhou originally resided only at Guanyin.
In the same rhyme, I reply to Jingqiu:
In the quiet chambers of the western hall at this ancient temple, one enjoys leisurely ease. One does not fall into the trap of "neither cultivation nor non-cultivation.
Yet I laugh at how, on a night of deep snow at Mount Ao, Xuefeng stubbornly insisted on questioning Yantou.
The Master Zang of Shimu’s coming and going are the same as not coming and going; within the waters of death at Pipphala Cave, the pivot of profound eloquence is vast and empty.
Only now does the path beneath the Shaolin gate truly open.

This Dharma talk for the Chan practitioner Shichuan is a single, direct transmission; it has never been circuitous. To say there is no circuitousness is already to fall into the seventh or eighth stage.
When Deshan saw a monk enter the gate, he would immediately strike him; when Linji saw a monk enter the gate, he would immediately shout at him.
Although this is called "seizing them by the face" and "directly handing it over," it is truly the foremost. [Other methods] are like dragging through mud and water;

thus it is said: "Even this is still a secondary phrase. A single movement of the eyes constitutes a deviation. If one asks about the essential meaning of Caoxi, it already becomes a secondary level of response. Although...
However, such a capacity is rare even today. For now, investigate this closely and continuously within the midst of daily activities:
while climbing mountains or crossing waters, eating or dressing, speaking or remaining silent, moving or staying still—do not allow for even a moment’s interruption.
Proceed until the five desires and eight winds have no place to enter; until everything is vivid and clear, without even a hair’s breadth of obstruction or hindrance.
This is still not the ultimate. One must simply "crack" and "shatter," undergo a great death once, and only then can one find the lifelong joy of fulfillment.
Thereafter, whether entering the Buddha-dharma or the realm of demons, whether entering the heterodox or the orthodox, all are equally the state of suchness.
Thus, one is able to extend a hand into the dust and toil of the world, responding to conditions to benefit sentient beings, serving as a banner of light for the末法 (mofa) age.
Zhaozhou’s “Before your parents were born, which one is your original face?”— this koan is a sharp sword that cuts through the net of birth and death,
a massive axe that fells the tree of afflictions. It lies precisely within the moments of turning, moving, bowing, and rising.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, investigate this closely and intimately, never forgetting it for even a moment. As days pass and years deepen, it will naturally become pure and unified;

without being raised, it is itself raised; without being brought forth, it is itself brought forth. From the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, the entire body is nothing but this one *huatou*.
When you reach such a state, seek even a single thread of the former dust-laden delusions and find that not a trace of their arising can be found.

It cannot be grasped. Suddenly, like a lacquer bucket whose bottom has fallen out, the boundaries of past and future are severed; only then does one realize that the Great Sage was originally in Sizhou.
Nevertheless, there remains one final point. The laywoman Gui Zhengzhen of Tushun, having cultivated wholesome seeds in past lives, possesses deep faith in this one matter of her own person.
She sent paper requesting instruction, so I have transcribed these former words to bestow upon her.
He said to Pan Zhengzhi:
"If one discusses this matter, it is like the great void; fundamentally it has no form or appearance. How could it be characterized by blue, yellow, red, white, long, or short?"
It may be short, broad, or narrow, yet it can be compared and illustrated; yet it has no fixed location—how could it be reached by running, racing, or exhaustive searching?
It has no phenomena or principles—how could it be approximated through grand discourse, erudite debate, or the dazzling display of intellectual views?
It has no profound mysteries—how could it be grasped by those of sharp faculties and superior capacity who seek to clarify the three by citing the one?

Yet one is able to chew and swallow it. Even if one reaches the point where forms and appearances have vanished, locations are empty, phenomena and principles have perished, and the profound mystery is utterly transcendent—only to emerge from such a state by means of intellectual effort—one is still merely a "consciousness-man" playing with the spirit.

Even if you do not act in this way at all, but instead possess another path for turning about, you are still a spirit clinging to the grass and trees. Nevertheless, if one is a person who has attained [realization], they turn with effortless ease.
The ground is naturally such that everywhere one returns to the source, and at every turn one accords with the path. Things and self are a single wondrousness; environment and wisdom are as one.
Throughout the entire earth, there is not even a hair’s breadth that acts as an obstruction or hindrance. Even if you attain such a state, you have still not yet accorded with this matter.
Have you not seen how Master Sanjiao addressed the assembly, saying: "If we discuss this matter, it is beyond the eyebrows."
It was already missed long ago. At that time, Magu stepped out from the assembly and said, "I do not ask about what was missed;
what is this matter? Sanjiao said, "It has been missed. Magu then overturned the meditation seat, and Sanjiao struck him.
Only with such a style can one truly shoulder this matter. It is like the spark struck from flint, like a flash of lightning—how could it allow for deliberation?
The lay practitioner Pan Zhengzhi of Lianchuan, whose refined sobriquet is Yiru, is earnest and diligent, possessing the resolve to shoulder this matter;

he will certainly not rest until he has undergone one more "turning over of the ground" (*dizhuǎn*). Once he has undergone this turning over of the ground, there is no doubt that what was previously discussed will swiftly be entrusted to him.
Thus it is said: "If a person studies the Way but does not practice the Way, ten thousand ways..."
Deceptive objects vie with one another to arise; when the sword of wisdom emerges, not a single thing remains. Before clarity has appeared, darkness is already bright.
For now, what do you call this "sword of wisdom"? Do not raise it before those who possess wisdom; do not speak of it before those who lack it.

This reveals the True Dharma Eye Treasury (Shōbōgenzō) of profound and correct practice. Since the World-Honored One held up the flower and Kāśyapa smiled, it was transmitted from one to another until it reached Bodhidharma, who first transmitted this Way to this land as the First Patriarch. It was subsequently transmitted to Caoqi.
Consequently, it branched out and spread throughout the world. All of these were transmitted mind-to-mind and handed down vessel-to-vessel, without the slightest error.
They were all individuals of great capacity who could discern the subtlest nuances; even before a hair had moved, they were already able to grasp the essence.
How could they be compared to teachers of words or scholars of doctrine, who divide texts into chapters and sentences?
Is it not the case that those who transmit [the Dharma] through analytical dissection, clever rhetoric, and circuitous metaphors are doing so? Thus it is said:

"In our school there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others. Yet in later generations, as the Dharma has shifted with the times and the faculties of beings have gradually become dull and inferior, one was eventually compelled to instruct them to hold a *huatou* (critical phrase);
this too was done out of necessity. The lay practitioner Shen Zhengxing of Lianchuan has deep faith in this Way.
Investigate the "Mu" (無) kōan of Master Zhaozhou. I request a word to serve as a warning. Therefore, I say:

This "Mu" is a hair-piercing sword. You must take all that arises and ceases within the consciousness of the mind—which is like a tangled skein—and cut it with a single stroke so that it never continues again. Constantly keep it vivid and distinct. Then...

The Buddha-nature inherently present does not depart from a single thought; it manifests naturally and expansively before one. Chen Zhengxing, you should apply yourself with vigor and alertness during the examination within the room.
The Master gave this discourse: "The source of the Way is not far off; where does it lie? Why did the Patriarch come from the West?
There is no tree of Bodhi; who established its name?"
A monk asked, "What is a guest within guests? The Master said, "Leaning on a staff by another's gate. The monk asked, "What is a host within guests?
The Master said, "Leaning against a pillar in front of the hall. The monk asked, "What is a guest within the host? The Master said:
"Life and nature belong to another. The monk asked, "What is the master among masters? The Master said, "Holding a vajra in his hand.
Layman Hu Juehai asked, "What is the matter regarding the gate of the patch-robed monks? The Master said, "You are a person of the secular world."
"How can one understand the affairs of the patch-robed monks' school? He asked again, "What are the affairs of the School of the Patriarchs?
The Master said, "I am busy today and have no leisure to explain the affairs of the School of the Patriarchs to you. As Hu hesitated, the Master shouted at him and drove him out.
One day, as the Master saw a monk walking past in the courtyard, he called out in a stern voice, "The eaves of the roof are collapsing!
The monk looked up in alarm and fear. The Master said, "A hawk has flown off to Silla."
As soon as the Master saw the monk enter the gate, he said, "You fellow who treads upon prefectures and counties—your heels deserve thirty blows!
The monk said, "I have not even asked a question, yet I have already been granted these blows. The Master said, "Wait until you open your mouth."

"What can you do? The monk hesitated, and the Master immediately shouted him out. A monk came to visit; as he was about to unfold his sitting cloth (*zuoju*), the Master said, "In my place, there is no leftover soup or stale rice;
there is no need to use up your worn-out cooking cloth. The monk said, "Out of compassion, Master, please accept my prostrations.
The Master said, "The green stone pillar in front of the gate has fallen over laughing. A monk asked for instruction, citing a past case: "In the past, a monk asked Ba[izhang]..."

Ling asked the Master, "Regarding the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings, are they the same or different? Baling said, "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree; when the duck is cold, it goes down into the water.

The Master asked, "What is the meaning of this? The monk said, "I ask you, Master. The monk asked again, "Regarding the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings, are they the same or different?
The Master said, "A chipped ceramic bowl and a broken rush fan. The monk said, "I do not understand. I hope the Master will be compassionate toward me."
The Master pointed and said, "A bowl is good for holding cakes; a fan is good for catching the breeze.
The monk hesitated, and the Master said in a stern voice, "To know through thinking and to understand through deliberation is the livelihood of ghosts. Get out!"

The Master asked the attendant, "When National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang called for his attendant three times a day, and the attendant responded 'Yes' each time, do you understand? The attendant said, 'It was simply because the Teacher’s heart was so earnest.
The Master said, 'If you understand it that way, you have not even dreamed of the National Teacher’s stench of sweat. The attendant said, 'I hope the Master will point this out for me. The Master...
He said: "Wait until Bowl-Basin Peak nods its head, and I shall tell you.
This was the postscript written for Jianzang by Beijian Wushan regarding his calligraphic manuscript.

The virtuous ancestors of our school who excelled in poetry and prose did not do so out of self-aggrandizement; rather, they sought to expound the principles of the Buddha and awaken the minds of others.
Mingjiao said, "When masters of Chan cultivate literary works, it is certainly not for nothing; their aim is to lead people's hearts to penetrate the principles of the Buddha.
This is precisely what is meant. Now, observing the response to the poem by Master Xiashi to Meipo, he says: "Sitting until one forgets..."
Regarding the phrase "the place": it is desolate and resembles its former state. It is just like tossing a brick in a bustling marketplace; only when it strikes someone does one truly know.
This is the verse Master Xiangyan presented to Attendant Bin, which was composed for the sake of Master Zhi of Haizang.
His realization is precise and his insight is clear; every word he utters issues forth from that which is inherently present.

Manifesting from the outset no intention regarding skill or clumsiness, he was thus able to cut off the paths of conceptual meaning and forget emotional designations, allowing no room for mental fixations to settle.

Among the venerable masters of recent times, Wansong Xingxiu (Hengchuan Wushang) is such an example. Some say that when the Master takes up and presents [the kōan] or offers praise and instruction, it must be as towering as a cliff or a mountain peak;

he strives to stand out uniquely to reflect upon the ancients and insists on being entirely authentic. This, however, is to give rise to a deliberate mind and intentional effort—how could this possibly accord with the directness [of the Way]?

To point out the Way in such a manner is a grave misrepresentation of the Master. Because the Abbot Zhou requested a title for the five verses he presented to Attendant Bin, I have appended my humble views to the end.
The Mirror of the Meaning of the Heart Sūtra by Master Boyuan Shen.
I have examined the *Mirror of the Meaning of the Heart Sūtra* composed by Master Qianxi. Its prose and diction are concise and essential;

it abridges the prolixity of various masters while expanding upon their brevities. It adjudicates among diverse interpretations and scrutinizes them to return to the ultimate principle. It is as if one were drawing from the *Bodhisattva-sambhāra*.

In this treatise, it is particularly appropriate that the wisdom of realization is shown to encompass the remaining perfections. Truly, if a student were to contemplate this once, it would be like holding up a bright mirror, wherein the myriad phenomena are clearly revealed.
Would it not be fitting to title this "The Mirror of Meaning"? It is just as in our own school, with the Venerable Master Yongming.
Synthesizing the various schools, it is titled the *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the School). As this book circulates within the religious community, how could its contribution be considered minor?
Nevertheless, there is a single character therein that has never been uttered. Tell me, what character is it?
Those everywhere who possess the discerning eye of the Dharma, please point it out.
The Inner Secretary Wei and the Court Historian Song [have written this].

Following the preface to the *Sengzhe yongming lüshi xu*, scholars of all schools have universally regarded the Vinaya as their primary task. How difficult it is to be a master who propagates the Vinaya!

Among those whose teachings have entered this land and may be revered as orthodox, there are but a few—namely, those from Beitaishan, Nanshan, and Lingzhi. The study of the Vinaya is truly a rare and difficult achievement.
This is indeed self-evident. It is clear that his understanding and practice were lofty; thus, the people of Wu and Yue revered him as their patriarchal teacher.

When the Imperial Secretariat Official Wei Su and the Court Historian Song Lian composed prefaces to praise him, it was truly only fitting. The Historian was refined in Buddhist principles and presented the Vinaya studies in systematic detail, providing an especially thorough account of their origins and development.
Once this literature has been transmitted, the poem by Liu Zhongxun (Liu Zhouhou) sent to Master Jun will no longer [be the sole record].

Thus, he has attained singular excellence surpassing those who came before. When I traveled to Kaiyuan to pay my respects at the preceptor of the ordination platform, I first made his acquaintance and was fortunate enough to examine two of his writings;
therefore, I have inscribed this at the end.

Regarding the words from Master Qiong’s small public discourse (xiaocan) at Yunfeng, the Venerable Ancestor Miaoxi, while in the assembly of Master Zhantang, took up a brush and wrote down the words of Yunfeng to admonish himself.
Zhantang said, "This man will surely one day shoulder heavy responsibilities and travel great distances. Subsequently, he resided once at Mount Mao and twice at Jingwu.
He bestowed the great rain of the Dharma, drawing forth the extraordinary patch-robed monks of the world and winning the joyful submission of renowned dukes and great scholars.
His realization accorded with the imperial heart, and he revived the Linji lineage. Alas! How clear and efficacious was Tanzhang’s insight!
He was like Xiao He recognizing Han Xin, or Zeng Kai recognizing Ye Yong. In these times, the monastic communities have declined; fledgling practitioners spend their days [in negligence].
Tan Wugen, would he ever be willing to act like Miaoxi by creating karmic conditions for the assembly? Or was it merely to record ancient words for his own admonition?
I admire the Chan practitioner Qiong for his aspiration to emulate the ancients; therefore, I have recorded this on the left side.
After this copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* written in ink on paper by Shu-ben:
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.

To hear it and have faith without opposition already surpasses the merit of giving away the seven treasures and one’s own body and life three times over as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; how much more so to write it!
Is this not for those who transcribe, uphold, read, and recite? The lay devotee (upāsaka) Yibuke Shubun of Wumen has long maintained the practice of recitation;

that he now transcribes it once more allows us to know his profound faith in the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Onlookers will surely say that this must serve as a condition for his future attainment of Buddhahood—how could it be compared to worldly merit?
Yet they fail to realize that even before the pen was raised, he had already attained Buddhahood.
If you do not believe this, try entering the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* (Sunlight Samādhi) and inquire of Maitreya in Tuṣita.
This was written by Wen Riguang based on the words of Mahāmati.

While in a state of tranquility, I once read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, reaching the passage: "As for killing their bodies and lives, or eating their flesh, throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust..."
The cycle of devouring and being devoured is like a turning wheel, where high and low alternate; one’s hair stands on end at the mere thought of it.

Now, observing the words of the ancient patriarchs of Wondrous Joy (*Abhirati*), it is said: "The cycle of rebirth is quickly changing its head and face; it occurs in but a single instant. Is this not true?
Buddhas and patriarchs share the same tongue and the same compassion. Yet sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age merely crave its flavor and fail to perceive it.
To disregard the suffering of saṃsāra and indulge in slaughter is not only self-destruction and self-abandonment, but a willing acceptance of evil retribution;
it betrays the heart of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to a great degree. One should observe these words daily and show them to others; keep them within one’s mind with silent composure.

If one contemplates it at this time, could it not be that one thereby accords with the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Having had the honor of viewing it, I have thus written this afterword to record the date.
Postscript to the Blood-Scriptured *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

At the request of Hu Bencheng, Wang Fuyuan of Lianchuan—having long since resolved his mind—punctured his own flesh to transcribe the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Upon reaching the eighth fascicle, he passed away.
His friend Hu Bencheng continued the transcription to completion. Having returned to Shuangjiang, he paid obeisance with deep longing and made this request.
I have observed this later development. Alas! Zhang Fangping, in a previous life, had not finished copying the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*;

he was reborn to continue the transcription, thereby fulfilling his original vow. Now Wang Fuyuan had not finished copying the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* when he passed away; his friend Hu Bencheng continued the transcription.
Yet for Fuyuan, there was no need to be reborn; he fulfilled his vow and attained true liberation in this very body.
Fuyuan can truly be called a spiritual friend who understood the mind. How could he be compared to those who merely hung their swords upon the trees at their graves?

Inscription for the Blood-Script *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* by Zhèngzhì of Liànchuān. Having drawn blood to serve as ink and transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, [Zhèngzhì] performed prostrations and requested an inscription for its conclusion.
He then said: "Within the scripture it is stated that Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, together with twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all..."
Before the Buddha, they made this vow: "May the World-Honored One not be concerned;

after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall exert the power of great patience to read, recite, uphold, explain, and transcribe this sutra, making various kinds of offerings and not sparing our own bodies or lives.
"Excellent, householder! You are indeed among those twenty thousand bodhisattvas who have returned by the power of their vows."

Indeed it is so. Otherwise, how could one, amidst the Dharma of the Final Age, give rise to the power of great forbearance and, disregarding body and life, pierce their own blood for ink to transcribe this sutra?
Nevertheless, before the golden needle is lowered and the hair-tip brush is raised, this sutra is fundamentally and inherently complete.
If one were to perceive this sutra only after the strokes and dots have already taken form, it would be like [seeking the sword]... [the sword].
It has been a long time since [the master] passed away. Following the death of the Dongshan Abbot Kecheng,
his grandson Jing’an obtained a memorial for him composed by Lord Yao, the Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince.
I have appended the master’s own calligraphic manuscript of his *Pure Land Sūtra, Images, and Praises* to the end of this biography.

I have bound them together into a single scroll with the intention that those who read the biography may come to know the deeds of our patriarch, and by reading the praises, they may realize that the words of the biography are not false.
Furthermore, he has requested a preface for the end of this work. Upon reading the biography and the praises, I believe that the Master of Contemplation truly possessed such words as these.
His conduct was such that it could not be compared to the common stream of those who merely study words.
Was he perhaps a Bodhisattva from the Land of Lotus Flowers, who, by the power of his vows, came here to guide the deluded masses and lead them together to birth in the Pure Land?

If not, why were his practice and understanding so preeminent, yet at only thirty-two years of age, he has already departed for eternity? Alas! The Dharma-vehicle is in decline, and monks are many [in number but few in virtue].

Amidst such profusion, it is difficult to find one who can truly emulate a successor to the Master. It is said that in recent times there has been but one such person; how could this be considered excessive praise?
Therefore, I have not declined to compose this record, as set forth below.
Postscript to the Stele Inscription for the Chan Master Hui Wujin-zang:

As for those who are śramaṇas, their nobility lies in clarifying the essence of the Buddha-mind and ensuring that practice and understanding are in accord. Among those who have become śramaṇas in recent times, some possess practice but lack understanding;

some possess understanding but lack practice; and some possess neither practice nor understanding. Only occasionally is there one who is fully endowed with both practice and understanding—such as he [the subject of this inscription].

Is there anyone capable of clarifying the essential school of the Buddha’s mind? As for one who possesses both practice and understanding and is thus able to clarify the essential school of the Buddha’s mind—is it not the Abbot Huì Wújin of Zhōngwú?
Wújin maintains a discipline as pure as ice; he is diligent and courageous in meditation and recitation.
He drew blood to transcribe the various Mahāyāna sūtras, enduring bitter hardship and simple fare while fully performing all the duties within the Triple Gem, persevering without slackening.

Is this not the practice of the Way? Studying the teachings and contemplation in the ancient courtyard and listening to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in the chamber of Master Rong—both represent points of entry;

is this not the attainment of understanding? Furthermore, following Master Xing from Mount Huqiu to investigate the purport of the "Separate Transmission"—is this not clarifying the Buddha-mind lineage?
These three matters are the tasks of great beings who transcend the world, and Wujin possessed them all.
As for his passing from life into death and attaining great mastery (*mahāvaśitā*), it was indeed only natural. That he manifested his body as a mass of fire was his playful exercise of *samādhi*;
that relics emerged from the ashes was the manifest verification of his practice. How could this be considered extraordinary?
Dharma Master Qúan-ān composed a biography of his conduct, and my elder brother Fǎhuàn inscribed his stūpa; truly, this is comparable to Cáo Yōng composing the epitaph for Guō Línzhī.
The inscriptions on the memorial steles for the patriarchs are no different. When a petty śramaṇa contemplates them, his forehead cannot help but break into a cold sweat.
Following the verses of lamentation written for the late laywoman Zhang, I reflect that the spirit of the mind is subtle and wondrous, inconceivable;
it penetrates the three periods of time and encompasses the ten voids, containing the hundred realms and gathering all within it.
All phenomena—every single thing, in every place—are fully manifest. In every world-system and every atom, how could there ever be any separation?
As for the dharmas of the mundane and supramundane worlds, apart from the mind, how could there be even a single thread or speck of dust that can be found elsewhere?
After the passing of his wife, Zhang Shi Benning, the lay practitioner Wang Bendao of Wumen collected the volumes of lamentation verses composed by masters from various quarters.

Please provide an explanation for this later. I then examined it thoroughly. As for the conduct of the Zhang family during their lifetime and the radiance that manifested after their deaths, these have all been fully elaborated elsewhere.

As for the appearance of Buddha images on the cotton used to wipe the scriptures and the manifestation of auspicious signs in the lamp flames, to claim these were moved by their sincerity and faith is not correct;
if they were, then there would be phenomena existing apart from the mind. Therefore, I shall verify this with a small example.
Verse: Head to head, there is no gap; place to place, there is no deviation. Outside the mind, there is no dharma; it is the continuous flame of the Buddha’s lamp. This is the fundamental Way.

Having perused the Great Canon and investigated the study of the mind, you must have already attained a profound understanding of Buddhist principles; you should now consider this matter for yourself.
The four venerable masters— Xieshi, Xianan, Meizhou, and Pushe—
manifested in their conduct all manner of scriptural recitations, incantations, protective rites, crafts, and various arts and skills, thereby bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
Therefore, the ancestral masters attained a state of intimacy and possessed a clarity of vision.

Their expressions—whether in prose, poetry, lyrics, or hymns, or even in jest, laughter, scolding, rebukes, shouts, or blows—were nothing other than revelations of the ultimate point to guide and receive those who came to study.
What else could this be? These are the surviving writings of four venerable elders, now preserved by Xiangchu, the current abbot of Wanshou Monastery in Central Wu.
Master Xuán has treasured this and preserved it here. All who unroll these pages should likewise observe it in this manner.
If one merely prizes the elegance of the phrasing and the propriety of the calligraphy, it is like a blind man feeling an elephant;
he only pursues its head, tail, ears, tusks, trunk, and feet. How could such a person ever recognize the elephant’s entire form?

The *Blood-Scriptured Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Skin was flayed for paper; bones were split for pens; blood was pricked for ink. Thus the scriptures were transcribed, accumulating as high as Mount Sumeru.
For the sake of honoring the Dharma, they did not spare their own bodies or lives. But tell me, what is this Dharma? It is the seven locations and nine assemblies.
"Is it this Dharma spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? Is it this sound spontaneously emerging from the jeweled nets of the Cloud Terrace?

Or is it this Dharma spoken by the fifty-three spiritual friends to Sudhana? If one is a truly sharp and discerning monk, one will immediately comprehend that what was spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas across the seven locations and nine assemblies is not the Dharma, nor is it the [sound from] the Cloud Terrace.
The jewel net spontaneously produces sounds; these are not the Dharma. The fifty-three spiritual friends described by Sudhana are not the Dharma.
Since none of these are the Dharma, what, after all, can be called the Dharma? Before those with clear eyes, one must not speak erroneously.
The monk Liji of Zhongwu, who once served as the librarian at Linggu Monastery, resolved to draw blood from his own body.

I copied the Avataṃsaka Sūtra in order to repay the profound kindness of my parents for their tireless labor. Having obtained this opportunity for contemplation, I have recorded it at the end of the volume.

Now tell me: is this true diligence, or is it not true diligence? Is this called the true Dharma, or is it not called the true Dharma? You must know!
True diligence and the true Dharma are perfectly clear and manifest even before one has opened their mouth or raised a brush.
The assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly present, undispersed. If you seek it within sounds or written characters, the hawk has already flown past to Silla.

It is like the Yanglan and Zuoli marshes—a minor Buddhist service.
The Venerable Jing covered the coffin. When the mind is pure for a single thought-moment, birth and death are forever severed.
The phrase "sweeping along with the waves," the phrase "cutting off all currents," and the phrase "the casket covers heaven and earth"—none need be brought forth at all.
The Venerable Fire, the new head of the community, has already served for many years; he is not one who has newly entered the monastic groves.
As for the great matter of birth and death, if it remains unclarified, listen now as the flames preach the Dharma for you.
The fire of Elder Jing was pure; his wondrous wisdom was perfectly complete, its essence inherently empty and tranquil. His passage from birth to death was like fire consuming ice.

As for the fire of Guest Monk Mao, he had not yet realized that guest-dust afflictions were adventitious. Once Mao understood the one true reality, he cleared the universe wide open, until even the flames leaping from dead firewood raised a true roar.
The head seat Daxingkong’s fire: chanting praises atop the bell tower, growing vegetables beneath his bed—directly penetrating through, unimpeded by birth and death.
The true fire of nature; the true emptiness of nature’s fire. A gnat swallows the peak of Mount Sumeru.
Master Cheng presides over the fire; as he casts down the fragments of wood, the waves of the Dharma-realm settle into clarity. He thoroughly realizes there is neither Buddha nor Patriarch;

Tea from the island in the middle of Jiangxin Lake: seeing illusion and awakening to non-arising—this is the second capacity.

Before the Sun of Wisdom, Qitan locked the cave with stone; before Peak Jiliu, he personally witnessed the illusion dissolve.
Eight *liang* in his left eye, he held a black bamboo staff in the Hall of Wisdom; half a *jin* in his right eye, he shattered the barrier of birth-and-death and cut off the path to nirvana.
When the Purple Emperor pressed down upon the five-colored unicorn, he casually snapped the golden lock asunder.

Former Abbot of the Left in the Office of the Monastic Registrar, Venerable Heshang Quan’an, turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma in the region of Wu, like the sun at its zenith with no shadow cast askew;

Patterns form spontaneously; melting the mundane and forging the sacred occurs in a single instant. Entering death and transcending birth is like a game.
Great assembly, do you know where Master Quanan’s wondrous function lay throughout his life? His hand moves freely across the face of reality, distinguishing him from others:
when he brings forth mugwort soup, it is nothing other than tea.
The hall master, the storehouse keeper, the attendants, and those who tend the fires; the rice-hammering in the mill—these are matters on the shore of birth and death.
Announcing to the assembly in the corridors—this too is a matter on the shore of birth and death. How can one emerge from birth and death? From two comes one; do not even cling to that one.
